Hey @yongruilin is the window for 1.36 still opened? We would really like to switch [FluxCD](https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/issues/5761) to the `events.k8s.io/v1` API and the missing `AnnotatedEventf` is blocking us. 

Thanks!

Friendly ping on this PR for `client-go/tools/events`.

This change adds `AnnotatedEventf` to the new events API so callers can attach annotations at event creation time, matching the capability that already exists in the legacy recorder API. It is currently blocking [FluxCD’s](https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/issues/5761) move to `events.k8s.io/v1`.

/cc @dgrisonnet @richabanker 
would you mind taking another look from the tools/events side?
/assign @aojea 
since Prow shows approval is needed from both `staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/OWNERS` and `pkg/registry/core/service/OWNERS`, I’d really appreciate your review/approval if this looks good.

Thanks! 😃

I tried to go through the (long) history of comments on the [initial implementation of the new Events API](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/49112) and the [issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/383), didnt find any call outs for why annotations must not be supported for the new API, so I guess this is okay?

cc @dgrisonnet if you have more thoughts on this

Do you have a use-case in mind for these annotations?

To give a bit of background, there was multiple attempts to add this functionality to the new API, but none had a convincing use-case for it. I personally have some reservation because I think that if we need to add additional structured data to Events then they might not be the best vector for that information. For instance, logs might be better suited.
You can find my past comments about this topic here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124170#issuecomment-2067018354

@dgrisonnet annotations is how we enrich the events in [Flux CD](https://github.com/fluxcd), this is a core feature and without it we would break OTEL and may other observability features in Flux. For example, we have an annotation called `revision` that allows other Flux controllers to trace back a change to its origin in Git, the revision holds the Git commit SHA. Another example, we propagate annotations from OCI Artifacts to the events related to this source type, consumers (other controllers and event aggregators like Loki) use these annotations for filtering and grouping.

> @dgrisonnet annotations is how we enrich the events in [Flux CD](https://github.com/fluxcd), this is a core feature and without it we would break OTEL and may other observability features in Flux. For example, we have an annotation called `revision` that allows other Flux controllers to trace back a change to its origin in Git, the revision holds the Git commit SHA. Another example, we propagate annotations from OCI Artifacts to the events related to this source type, consumers (other controllers and event aggregators like Loki) use these annotations for filtering and grouping.

Also, allowing structured metadata in events is a basic requirement in most event features out there in the tech world

> Also, allowing structured metadata in events is a basic requirement in most event features out there in the tech world

Kubernetes Events are very different from the events you normally encounter in cloud native environments. To quote the official doc: "Events should be treated as informative, best-effort, supplemental data.". In Kubernetes, events were designed to be used as another vector of observability. They are meant to be human-readable and are not reliable enough to be used in event-driven systems.

I get your point, especially considering that Kubernetes produces structured logs now, but Events are meant to be consumed by humans only, so adding metadata might make less sense here than it normally does for events. That said, it could potentially be valid for visualization.

I might be misunderstanding something, but I feel like Flux is using these annotations as a shared metadata layer across signals. Events might not be the best medium for that especially considering that they are best practice and might be dropped by the client at any time.

Thanks for your feedback @dgrisonnet! 

I see as a concerning point the missing migration parity with the legacy API. If the new tools doesn't offer the same capability, it becomes difficult for those projects to migrate — they'd be moving to the recommended API but losing functionality in the process. I think for the new tool to be a viable replacement, it needs at least feature parity with the one it's replacing.

On the other hand, in my humble view, logs aren't a substitute for this use case. Events and logs serve different audiences. For a use case like Flux's — attaching a Git revision to a reconciliation event so downstream consumers can correlate the change —structured logs can't fill that role because they aren't associated with a Kubernetes object and can't be watched through the API.
/retest

Friendly reminder - Would love to get another look whenever you get a chance. Thanks! 😃
@richabanker @dgrisonnet

This change touches **client-go** interfaces, so looping in sig-api-machinery for visibility.

/sig api-machinery

/unassign @aojea

/cc @aojea @liggitt @apelisse  — would appreciate a look from the api-machinery side on the new `AnnotatedEventRecorder` interface and `EventRecorderAdapter` changes.

I wonder if, instead of doing this specifically for annotations (and opening ourselves for similar cases in the future for other custom fields), it'd be better to morph this into taking in user-defined object and merging those fields in, which should cover annotations and more?

Why do we need to extend the golang API just to add this helper? As you see in several comments is not something that is used internally, and we  already have problems with the client-go surface ... besides, external consumers that want to add annotations can perfectly do it themselves, no?

Thanks @rexagod and @aojea for the feedback!

@aojea — The challenge for external consumers is that the `EventRecorder`/`EventBroadcaster` pipeline doesn't expose a hook to modify the event between creation and submission — `Eventf` constructs the events/v1.Event internally and sends it asynchronously via the broadcaster. So callers can't "do it themselves" without either:

1. Bypassing the recorder entirely and creating events via the raw client (losing deduplication, series tracking, and the broadcaster's backpressure)
2. Using an `EventWatcher` to intercept and mutate events after the fact (racy, since the event may already be
submitted)

The legacy API (tools/record) already solved this with `AnnotatedEventf` — this PR is just bringing parity to the new
API so projects like FluxCD can migrate off the deprecated path.

@rexagod — A more generic approach (e.g., an `EventOption` functional pattern or an ObjectMeta override) is interesting
but would be a larger API design discussion. Would it make sense to land the minimal `AnnotatedEventf` for parity with
the legacy API now, and iterate toward a more generic pattern in a follow-up if there's demand for other fields? That
keeps the scope small and unblocks the migration path.

Happy to adjust the approach if there's a preferred direction. Would an `EventOption` pattern be a more suitable from the
API surface perspective?

>  attaching a Git revision to a reconciliation event so downstream consumers can correlate the change 

this is the main concern `Events should be treated as informative, best-effort, supplemental data` , if people is extending the events to build critical pipelines is more an argument to indicate why the first addition back in 1.11 was a bad idea we can not repeat rather than, let's allow people build logic on top of an unreliable source in a pub/sub like architecture on top of Events

I seriously do not understand this push back on allowing annotations for events. Even log lines are printed in JSON format to have structured fields, why can't a Kubernetes API called *Events* have the same? (It already does, but the Go package for sending events can't?) Also, I understand this has already been agreed upon in a recent SIG meeting.

> I seriously do not understand this push back on allowing annotations for events.

you can perfectly add annotations to events, you can add them, nothing stops doing that.

The discussion is about allowing to extend an official golang API to support an anti-pattern in kubernetes, like building a pub-sub architecture based on an API that is officially declared to not have delivery guarantees, so it will not work the way people think it will
Why do annotations imply pub/sub?

> Why do annotations imply pub/sub?

because that is inferred from the comments on the people requesting the functionality? using annotations to add metadata that triggers some business logic https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/blob/main/rfcs/0008-custom-event-metadata-from-annotations/README.md?plain=1 and integrate with other third party systems

It is important to mention that we already have a problem with the use of the golang API as a general library for the ecosystem that makes it super difficult to maintain and is causing a lot of problems with upgrades, see:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137270
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138351

Because it seems that this functionality is only used for your project , is not easy to just fork the event recorder and add the method there ? https://github.com/fluxcd/pkg/blob/f3ad4b56adec90eb5661af565cdebec997ad4bfb/runtime/events/recorder.go#L162

> using annotations to add metadata that triggers some business logic https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/blob/main/rfcs/0008-custom-event-metadata-from-annotations/README.md?plain=1 and integrate with other third party systems

That Flux RFC does not use the Kubernetes Event API for pub/sub at all. We simply implement the interface being proposed in this PR (the old one) to send the event to Kubernetes *and* fan out to our own endpoint (notification-controller). We are not subscribing to the Kubernetes API Server to listen for Events at all. The notification-controller fans out to dozens of systems, they all support structured metadata in their event payloads. The only system that gets the event sent from the source (with metadata a.k.a. annotations attched like all the others) is Kubernetes, and we send it there for the pure goal of observability related to the Flux object that generated the event, as that API is intended to be.

Fan out here: https://github.com/fluxcd/pkg/blob/f3ad4b56adec90eb5661af565cdebec997ad4bfb/runtime/events/recorder.go#L160-L271

Event providers here:
https://fluxcd.io/flux/components/notification/providers/#type

Let me put it this way, imagine that eventually Kubernetes decide to sample events by default, so you don't get some of the events ... will you ask the project to remove the sampling? 
I understand your desire, but you are asking the project to sign a contract that we can not commit to ... and the alternative is you just fork two files and build your own event recorder

> Let me put it this way, imagine that eventually Kubernetes decide to sample events by default, so you don't get some of the events ... will you ask the project to remove the sampling? I understand your desire, but you are asking the project to sign a contract that we can not commit to ... and the alternative is you just fork two files and build your own event recorder

Let me put it this way: every controller out there in the ecosystem *already uses* the upstream recorder. If you ship a breaking change like that, the impact will be very wide, so you should never do something like that, you should play nice. Are you saying that all the ecosystem controllers should switch to their own event recorder implementations today to avoid this kind of breaking change?

I didn;t mean to focus on the example per se, just on the effect and the importance on what we can support and what not, and the reason why we are pushing back in extending the library to offer a functionality that we can not support.

I perfectly understand pushing back on introducing API surface that cannot be supported, and I also perfectly understand protecting Go packages that are initially meant exclusively for supporting the development of the core project from sprawl. I'd love to simplify a few things in `github.com/fluxcd/pkg/ssa`, but tons of opensource projects are importing it. The SemVer for `fluxcd/pkg/ssa` is still not GA (v0.x), but we still avoid breaking changes there as if it was v1.x. I once had to argue this with someone, but in practice people are relying on it.

Also, you owe me no fair explanation, you are the one putting your time on the project health and we know how opensource can be unsustainable. A maintainer understands ownership.

But I don't understand *why* is this `a functionality that we can not support`. So far the aggregated reason still amounts to "I have a feeling we will want to break this interface one day, but I'm not sure why". You claim event metadata implies pub/sub, I have showed you that our use case is 100% not based on abusing the contract for pub/sub, but simply *following upstream best practices*. We firmly believe that events deserve structured metadata, like dozens of observability providers we integrate with. Kubernetes defends `.metadata.annotations` are supported for all API resources, including the new Event API. So the use case fits.

Would a redesign be acceptable? I can see how `Annotated` is just *one* feature in the Event API, so an option-oriented contract would probably be the best. If that's acceptable, we are perfectly fine migrating from the very specific `AnnotatedEventf` API to something more progressive, that was never an issue. We really just want a way to relay `.metadata.annotations` without having to write API machinery for such simple, basic feature in Kubernetes.

If that's acceptable, we are perfectly fine migrating from the very specific `AnnotatedEventf` API to something more progressive, that was never an issue. We really just want a way to relay `.metadata.annotations` without having to write API machinery for such simple, basic feature in Kubernetes.

to be honest, my only concern is the precedent and the blast radius, you know these kind of things always fire back and this discussion is a good example of [Hyrums law](https://www.hyrumslaw.com/) ... I think that the argument "already exists in the previous API so migration should offer the same capabiligies" is a reasonable argument , so we need to live with that... I spend some time trying to figure out another option and those do not look better than this one
